description_full: Arcos Dorados Holdings Inc. operates as a franchisee of McDonald's restaurants. It has the exclusive right to own, operate, and grant franchises of McDonald's restaurants in 21 countries and territories in Latin America and the Caribbean, including Argentina, Aruba, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Curacao, Ecuador, French Guiana, Guadeloupe, Martinique, Mexico, Panama, Peru, Puerto Rico, Trinidad and Tobago, Uruguay, the U.S. Virgin Islands of St. Croix and St. Thomas, and Venezuela. Arcos Dorados Holdings Inc. was founded in 2007 and is based in Montevideo, Uruguay.
ceo_bio: Mr. Luis  Raganato | Chief Executive Officer | Age 60
financial_summary: Arcos Dorados Holdings Inc. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $1.5B market cap on $4.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +9% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 17% against a 7% cost of capital, a 10-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $15M in free cash flow — roughly 0 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.40× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.3× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 27× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 3.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.94x).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 20% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 15% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 28% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 39% and a beta of 0.66, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.96 vs 5y 0.53), so read it loosely.
About $10.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 63% in the 2020 crash and 23% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 58% below its DCF fair value of $16.58, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 31%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $11.73 to $31.99 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Consumer Cyclical peers: cheaper on P/E 5.7 vs 19.3 and EV/EBITDA 5.6 vs 11.2, richer on P/FCF 98.1 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 39% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 1.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 10.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 9 covering analysts target $10.84 on average, 55% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 17% clears the cost of capital of 7.0% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.64).
It converts 0% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.40x.
ROE of 28% is amplified by 5.0x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.3x net debt to EBITDA ($422.3M of cash against $1.1B of debt), with interest covered 26.7x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.9% over 3 years, 18.7% over 5 years and 4.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 19%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 17.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.4x, 6.0% of sales), a maintenance pace.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 131.0% on average.
Analysts expect 9.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.5%), and institutions hold 52%.
It returns 3.4% a year to shareholders (4.0% in dividends).
The share count has grown 0.6% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
